newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Kabila leaves Lubumbashi for talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila leaves Lubumbashi for talks.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila left his headquarters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi at dawn on Friday for face-to-face talks at sea with Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, officials said.
"Kabila left this morning...at dawn for the Angolan capital Luanda, from where he will be moved by helicopter to a South African Navy ship for the talks," a security aide told Reuters.
South African President Nelson Mandela left for Congo meanwhile to act as host for the face-to-face peace talks between Mobutu and Kabila. He said he was hopeful of success.

Diplomatic sources earlier said South African officials worked into the early hours of Friday to try to keep on track plans to bring the two Zaireans together aboard the South African warship Outeniqua off the Congolese coast.

The South Africans were alarmed when Kabila made an unscheduled return to his headquarters in Lubumbashi on Thursday night instead of heading for Luanda, where South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki was awaiting him.
Mbeki, who will accompany Kabila onto the ship, travelled to Luanda on Thursday to join other dignitaries, including U.S. envoy Bill Richardson.

Mandela, who has staked his reputation on ending the Zairean conflict, told reporters on departure for the Congolese port of Pointe Noire: "Both President Mobutu and Mr Laurent Kabila are quite aware of the importance of this meeting.
"I believe that each one of them will make an effort to find a settlement that is acceptable to both of them as well as the masses of the people in Zaire."

Mobutu has lost control of most of Africa's third largest country but retains the capital Kinshasa. The leaders of the rebellion, which broke out in the east of Zaire last October, have vowed to take the city if the talks make no progress.
Confusion has abounded in the run-up to the Mobutu-Kabila meeting, with the two sides disagreeing on the purpose.
Mobutu's camp says the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. Kabila insists his rival must give up power after more than three decades in office.

"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," Kabila said in Lubumbashi. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away."
There was no indication Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, was ready to step down, although rebel "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha said the president had agreed to discuss his departure.
